title: Hallstatt's twin in China
hook: An Austrian lakeside village, copied almost house by house in Guangdong.
peek: Hallstatt is a tiny village on an Austrian lake, famous for its postcard looks. In 2012 a full-scale replica of its centre opened in Huizhou, in southern China, complete with a lake, a church tower and pastel houses.
lede: Hallstatt sits between a lake and a steep mountain in Austria's Salzkammergut, home to fewer than a thousand people. In 2012 a copy of its old centre opened in Huizhou, Guangdong, built as part of a housing development by the mining and metals company China Minmetals. It has its own lake, a market square and a copy of the church tower.

bullets.opening: A surprise for the real village
bullets.text: Some Hallstatt residents were caught off guard when news of the project spread. Feelings softened over time, and the village's mayor attended the opening of the replica.
The real Hallstatt grew rich on salt. Mining in the mountain above it goes back thousands of years and is still running, making it one of the oldest salt mines in the world.
Archaeologists named a whole period of early Iron Age Europe after finds made near the village in the 19th century, so its name appears in history textbooks far beyond Austria.
The copy is part of a wider trend in China. Tianducheng near Hangzhou has a smaller Eiffel Tower, and Thames Town near Shanghai has English-style streets and a mock-Tudor look.
Building something to look old is not new. English shop signs that say 'Ye Olde' are a similar wink at the past, based on a misread letter.

bullets.opening: Is a copy the real thing
bullets.text: Ise Shrine in Japan raises the same question from another side: it is rebuilt from new wood every 20 years and still counts as the original.
